chapter_title: Documentation, Reporting, and Communication for Site Characterization

sections.title: Objectives for Documentation and Reporting of Site Characterization
sections.summary: Documentation and reporting capture the knowledge gained, communicate results to those responsible for design and construction, and archive them for future design, construction and research; this chapter gives content for the report types of Chapter 2.
sections.body: The objective is to capture and record the knowledge gained from investigations. Reports are also the primary vehicle for communicating results to those responsible for design and construction, facilitating decisions, and they archive results for future design and construction and for advancing practice through research. Report forms were described in Chapter 2; this chapter gives guidance on their content. (p. 13-1)
key_points: Reports capture knowledge, communicate results and archive them (p. 13-1).
sections.applicability: Documentation and reporting of geotechnical site characterization for transportation design and construction projects

sections.title: Documentation and Reporting of Laboratory and Field Test Measurements
sections.summary: Geotechnical data reports give a brief narrative (context, scope, procedures) followed by logs, test reports, summary tables and factual observations, with a recommended table of contents (sections 1 to 7, Appendices A to H). Document methods, numbers, locations and depths, samples, dates, subcontractors, standards and deviations from plan; interpretations are not typically included.
sections.body: Laboratory and field measurements are generally documented in geotechnical data reports: a relatively brief narrative (context, scope, procedures) followed by field investigation logs, laboratory and field test reports, summary tables and other factual observations. Recommended contents: 1 Introduction; 2 Scope of Work; 3 Site Description; 4 Site Conditions, Geologic Setting and Topographic Information; 5 Scope and Procedures for Field Investigations (borings, in situ soundings, geophysics, exploration pits, groundwater); 6 Scope and Procedures for Laboratory Testing (index, design properties); 7 Results; Appendices A Field Investigation Plan, B Boring Logs, C In Situ Test Soundings, D Geophysical Measurements, E Exploration Pit Logs, F Groundwater Observations and Test Results, G Laboratory Test Results, H Historical Information (p. 13-2). Initial sections cover the project, purposes, planned features, requirements, site conditions, geology and peculiarities. Then the scope and procedures: methods; number, location and depths of borings, pits and soundings; sample types and frequency; dates; subcontractors; test types, numbers and standards; variations from conventional procedures; and differences between planned and actual scope (p. 13-3). Results go mainly in appendices (summary tables, individual test reports, final logs, piezometer and well installations, water levels, core photographs, geologic mapping, previous investigations) with a brief summary narrative. Data reports do not typically include interpretations but may include select graphs of collective measurements. (pp. 13-1 to 13-3)
key_points: Recommended table of contents: sections 1 to 7 and Appendices A to H (p. 13-2).
Document differences between planned and actual scope (p. 13-3).
Data reports do not typically include interpretations (p. 13-3).
sections.applicability: Content of geotechnical data reports documenting laboratory and field test measurements

sections.title: Documentation and Reporting for Design Parameters
sections.summary: Geotechnical design reports interpret subsurface conditions, document analyses and recommend design and construction, with a recommended table of contents. They identify each engineering unit (design cross-sections or profiles), give interpreted parameter values with their basis and uncertainty, address groundwater now and over time, and address hazards with mitigation.
sections.body: Design reports provide interpretations of subsurface conditions, procedures for and findings from analyses, and design and construction recommendations, plus much of the data report content (or incorporate it by reference). Recommended contents: 1 Introduction (project description, scope); 2 General Site Conditions (topography, geologic setting including seismicity, geotechnical hazards); 3 Summary of Field and Laboratory Investigations; 4 Interpretation of Design Parameters (stratigraphy, soil, rock, groundwater); 5 Recommendations for Design; 6 for Construction; 7 for Inspection, Instrumentation and Monitoring; Appendices A Site Plan with Boring Locations, B Interpreted Design Cross-sections, C Geotechnical Data Report. Combined data and design reports replace section 3 with data report items 5 to 7 and include its appendices (p. 13-4). Contents are tailored per project. Identify all soil and rock units of engineering significance with depths and extent (design cross-sections or profiles); document interpreted values for each unit, how they were established and indications or measures of their uncertainty; address groundwater for design and construction, at the time of investigation and how it may change; address hazards (source, likelihood of impact, mitigation of substantial risks) (p. 13-5). Recommendations commonly cover foundations, slopes, retaining walls, roadway and ground improvement, and construction (dewatering, staged construction, fill placement and compaction, inspection, instrumentation, load testing, monitoring). Appendices add interpreted stratigraphy drawings and tables of interpreted design values. (pp. 13-3 to 13-5)
key_points: Recommended design report table of contents, sections 1 to 7 and Appendices A to C (p. 13-4).
Document how parameter values were established and their uncertainty (p. 13-4).
Address groundwater conditions for both design and construction (p. 13-4).
Provide recommendations for mitigating substantial hazard risks (p. 13-5).
sections.applicability: Content of geotechnical design reports documenting interpreted design parameters and recommendations

sections.title: Geotechnical Baseline Reports
sections.summary: A geotechnical baseline report (GBR) sets a contractually binding interpretation of specific ground conditions: concise, without supporting interpretation or qualifiers like 'may' and 'should', with deviation criteria, differing site conditions and dispute provisions. Baseline only measurable parameters with greatest cost and schedule influence, never computed design values.
sections.body: GBRs establish a contractually binding interpretation of specific ground conditions for a project, different from data and design reports. Supporting information is not necessary or desirable; GBRs concisely define the interpretation and the means of assessing deviations during construction, usually with differing site conditions clauses and dispute resolution provisions; qualifying language such as 'may' and 'should' must be avoided (p. 13-5). GBRs should not baseline all conditions, only parameters with the greatest influence on cost and schedule (location and extent of important strata such as weak or highly permeable strata, shear strength of specific units, groundwater levels); not properties without direct construction impact nor computed design values such as side or tip resistance. All baselined parameters must be measurable, with documented measurement methods and deviation criteria; document inspection by contractor and owner; GBRs often include factual data reports but not much interpretive design-report content (p. 13-6). (pp. 13-5 to 13-6)
key_points: GBR: contractually binding interpretation of specific ground conditions (p. 13-5).
Avoid qualifying language such as 'may' and 'should' in GBRs (p. 13-5).
Baseline only parameters with the greatest influence on cost and schedule (p. 13-6).
Do not baseline computed design values such as side or tip resistance (p. 13-6).
All baselined parameters must be measurable (p. 13-6).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical baseline reports as contractual statements of ground conditions

sections.title: General Forms of Documentation for Site Characterization
sections.summary: Geotechnical reports commonly add graphical and tabular documentation to the narrative: site plans, final logs, laboratory test reports, design profiles and cross-sections, and instrumentation observations.
sections.body: Geotechnical reports commonly include graphical and tabular documentation of site characterization in addition to the narrative; sections 13.5.1 to 13.5.5 describe and recommend such documentation. (p. 13-6)
key_points: Graphical and tabular documentation accompanies the narrative (p. 13-6).
sections.applicability: Documentation and reporting of geotechnical site characterization for transportation design and construction projects

sections.title: Site Plans
sections.summary: Every data and design report needs a site location plan (Figure 13-1) with all borings and tests on a scaled plan, preferably with contours, a benchmark, north arrow, structures, roads and utilities, separate symbols with a legend for each exploration type, and a horizontal scale; GPS and GIS improve location accuracy.
sections.body: A site location plan should be provided in all geotechnical data and design reports (Figure 13-1, MnDOT, 2013, p. 13-7). Show all borings and field tests on a scaled site plan, preferably with topography, well-delineated elevation contours and an established benchmark, the direction of magnetic or true north, and important structures, roadways and utilities. GPS and GIS have dramatically improved location accuracy. Use separate symbols for each exploration method (borings, CPT soundings, test pits) with a clear legend, and present a horizontal scale. (pp. 13-6 to 13-7)
key_points: Site location plan in all geotechnical data and design reports (p. 13-6).
Separate symbols and a legend for each exploration method (p. 13-6).
Show a benchmark, north direction and horizontal scale (p. 13-6).
figures: Figure 13-1: Site plan showing locations of borings and in situ test soundings (MnDOT, 2013)
sections.applicability: Documentation and reporting of geotechnical site characterization for transportation design and construction projects

sections.title: Final Field Investigation Logs
sections.summary: Final logs of borings, soundings, test pits, wells and piezometers go in data reports (Figures 13-2 to 13-4), prepared with logging software and custom legends, and record location, dates, ground elevation, personnel, equipment and methods, sealing and closure, and groundwater observations.
sections.body: Final field investigation logs (borings, in situ soundings, test pits, monitoring wells, piezometers) belong in data reports, or design reports when no separate data report is prepared; example boring logs Figures 13-2 (Caltrans, 2010) and 13-3 (MnDOT, 2013), CPTU log Figure 13-4. Commercial software dramatically improves accuracy, efficiency and effectiveness; custom formats can include graphic logs, well details, data plots and legends of soil types, sampler and well symbols (p. 13-7). Logs should also give location, dates, ground elevation, personnel, equipment and methods, methods used to seal and close borings, and groundwater observations. (pp. 13-7 to 13-10)
key_points: Logs include location, dates, ground elevation, personnel, equipment and methods (p. 13-7).
Record methods used to seal and close borings and groundwater observations (p. 13-7).

sections.title: Laboratory Test Reports
sections.summary: Include individual laboratory test reports (Figure 13-5, UU triaxial) and summary tables (Figures 13-6 to 13-8: consolidation, UU, CU). Reports should add index properties, specimen dimensions, loading rate, failure loads, boring, sample and depth, a graphic and nomenclature; spreadsheet summaries feed collective interpretation.
sections.body: Data reports, and some design reports, should include appendices with individual laboratory test reports and summary tables by test type: Figure 13-5, a UU triaxial compression test report; Figures 13-6 to 13-8, summary tables for 1-D consolidation, UU triaxial and CU triaxial tests (these figures print in section 13.5.4's pages). Test reports should present primary results and additional measurements aiding collective interpretation: water content, dry unit weight, degree of saturation, Atterberg limits and specific gravity; specimen dimensions, loading rate and loads at failure; boring number, sample number and depth; a graphic and nomenclature. Summary tables, often from spreadsheets, allow direct comparison between tests and graphics for interpretation within strata (section 13.5.4). (p. 13-11)
key_points: Test reports include index properties, specimen dimensions, loading rate, failure loads (p. 13-11).
Record boring number, sample number and sample depth (p. 13-11).
sections.applicability: Documentation and reporting of geotechnical site characterization for transportation design and construction projects

sections.title: Design Profiles and Design Cross-sections
sections.summary: Design profiles (Figure 13-9) for localized or uniform areas and design cross-sections along alignments (Figure 13-10) show measurements, stratigraphic boundaries and parameter values with uncertainty (e.g., sigma_model), one profile per parameter; cross-sections use exaggerated vertical scales (1V:10H or 1V:20H), nearby borings, and dashed lines or question marks where uncertain.
sections.body: Reports normally include interpreted design profiles or design cross-sections. Design profiles (Figure 13-9) represent a localized area (a bridge pier) or practically uniform areas; design cross-sections show variability along a roadway or bridge alignment, with a few transverse sections at major foundations, cut slopes or high embankments (Figure 13-10) (p. 13-11). Figures 13-5 to 13-8 (cited in section 13.5.3) also print here. Profiles show available measurements, stratigraphic boundaries and interpreted values, preferably numerical with uncertainty (e.g., the model uncertainty, sigma_model); separate profiles per parameter; duplicate graphics at different scales where values span a large range (p. 13-15). Cross-sections use a scale suited to depth and length, commonly an exaggerated vertical scale [1(V):10(H) or 1(V):20(H)], present important units, show nearby borings to distinguish well-defined from interpreted stratigraphy, and use dashed interfaces or question marks where uncertain (p. 13-16). (pp. 13-11 to 13-16)
key_points: Design profiles for localized or practically uniform areas (p. 13-11).
Show parameter values with uncertainty, e.g., sigma_model (p. 13-15).
Separate profiles for each relevant design parameter (p. 13-15).
Exaggerated vertical scale, e.g., 1(V):10(H) or 1(V):20(H) (p. 13-16).
Dashed lines or question marks where stratigraphy is uncertain (p. 13-16).

sections.title: Observations from Field Instrumentation
sections.summary: Report instrumentation observations, e.g., piezometer or well groundwater records and inclinometer or settlement plate deformations; near a waterway, plot its level with groundwater levels (Figure 13-11).
sections.body: Data and design reports should document observations from field instrumentation if available: groundwater from monitoring wells or piezometers, deformations from slope inclinometers or settlement plates. Figure 13-11 shows piezometer pore pressure fluctuations over time; near a stream or other waterway, include the waterway level in the plot for comparison. (p. 13-16)
key_points: Near a waterway, plot its level with measured groundwater levels (p. 13-16).

sections.title: Geotechnical Data Management Systems
sections.summary: Geotechnical data management systems (proprietary, in-house or commercial) standardize how subsurface and construction data, always with location, are controlled and exchanged. The U.S. standard DIGGS is an XML exchange format; DIGGS 2.0b (May 2016) is being implemented and is expected to replace the AGS standard in the U.K.
sections.body: Incorporating measurements into geotechnical data management systems has become part of reporting. Most agencies use proprietary systems, in-house or commercial, some mature, others based on scanned documents. Data management refers to a data architecture and transfer standard synchronizing how subsurface and construction data are controlled, accessed and shared among users, programs and devices (log software, field and laboratory acquisition equipment, analysis software), for drilling and sampling, in situ testing, geophysics, laboratory testing and construction data; location data accompany all geotechnical information. In the U.S. the Data Interchange for Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Specialists (DIGGS) standard, an XML data exchange format, lets compliant programs share location-based data, e.g., a contractor's CPT sounding read by an agency's different program without loss of information or confusion of units. DIGGS 2.0b was released in May 2016 and is being implemented by vendors; intended as an international standard, it is anticipated to be adopted by the AGS in the United Kingdom, replacing the current AGS standard. (p. 13-17)
key_points: Most agencies use proprietary geotechnical management systems (p. 13-17).
Location data included with all geotechnical information (p. 13-17).
DIGGS is an XML data exchange format (p. 13-17).
DIGGS 2.0b released in May 2016 (p. 13-17).
sections.applicability: Geotechnical data management systems and the DIGGS data interchange standard
